The raid took place overnight on 22-23 March at the Magnani Rocca Foundation, about 12 miles (19km) from Parma, after a series of high-profile thefts from other European museums. Police released footage showing two masked burglars entering through a window, grabbing the three paintings from the wall and immediately leaving the building, in an operation that took less than three minutes. The recovered works are Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, which authorities said was valued at about $7m (£5.2m), Renoir’s Fish, valued at $3.5m, and Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace, valued at $23,000. A statement from the Italian Carabinieri’s art recovery squad said the paintings were found during searches ordered by prosecutors, but gave no further details. The investigation is continuing. View image in fullscreen Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, valued at about $7m. Photograph: Fondazione Magnani Rocca/Reuters On Thursday, civil police in São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, said they had recovered eight Matisse illustrations that were stolen from a library on 7 December last year. The works, created for the limited-edition art book Jazz and with a combined estimated value of about $200,000, had been stolen by two thieves who, on the final day of an exhibition, overpowered a security guard and an elderly couple visiting the library before fleeing on foot. Police said they believed the theft had been ordered by Laéssio Rodrigues de Oliveira, 53, regarded as one of Brazil’s most prominent art thieves, who has been in custody since April after being arrested in connection with another case. Police found the works at a home in São Bernardo do Campo, on the outskirts of São Paulo, and said they were in good condition. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The Matisse illustrations recovered by Brazilian police. Photograph: São Paulo police press office/AFP/Getty Images Photographs released by officers showed the illustrations laid out on a bed beside a .32 revolver that police said belonged to João Paulo Linhares de Araújo, 44, who was at the property and was arrested. Police said he had been storing the Matisse works on behalf of people accused of involvement in the theft. Three other people had previously been arrested in connection with the case. The works were returned to the library on Thursday. During the robbery, the thieves also took five engravings by the Brazilian artist Candido Portinari, which have not yet been recovered. Police said they suspected they had been sold. Photograph: Worcester Police Department Massachusetts Massachusetts woman suspected of killing police officer husband found dead Karen Solomon had been missing for six days after her husband Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home Associated Press Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.56 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 19.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead on Monday, six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said. Karen Solomon, an advocate who called for improvements and greater awareness of police mental health issues, had disappeared after Worcester police officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home just before 5.30am on 18 August. Officials had named Karen Solomon a suspect and said she was believed to be armed. “We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred,” the Worcester police chief, Paul Saucier, said at a news conference Monday. Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman’s corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon. A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it. On 19 August, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple’s home and found her husband’s body. Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said. Worcester county district attorney Joseph Early Jr said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband’s death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Arrest warrant issued for wife of Massachusetts officer found dead at home Read more Police handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple’s Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6km) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs. Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First Help, which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books – Hearts Beneath the Badge and The Price They Pay – about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders. In a 2020 interview on the Dr Phil show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives. In a statement read by Saucier during Monday’s news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers. “The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless,” the family said. “The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.” A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as “a tremendous human being” who was like family. He described Ratcliffe’s meeting with Russian intelligence chief Sergey Naryshkin as a standard procedure. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 27, 2026, 10:03 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A photo illustration shows US President Donald Trump alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin on Feb. 21, 2020. (Photo by Jim Watson and Emmanuel Dunand / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip US President Donald Trump dismissed the possibility of Russia attacking NATO countries while rejecting reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin against such a move. Trump made the remarks in a phone interview with Axios on Thursday, Aug. 27, after several media outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and Politico , reported on Wednesday, Aug. 26, that Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25, to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against attacking a NATO member. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year,” Trump said, adding that “they have a very good relationship.” “There was no message and there was nothing unusual,” he continued. “I am not concerned… at all. There is no problem.” Advertisement Russia confirms CIA meeting According to Axios, Naryshkin confirmed Thursday that he met Ratcliffe during his trip to Moscow. He described their discussions as a regular part of intelligence work and said there was “nothing out of the ordinary.” According to several media outlets, US intelligence assessments had focused on possible threats to the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – amid concerns that Moscow could seek to test NATO’s resolve through a limited incursion or a different kind of provocation, such as a cyberattack or hybrid warfare. Other Topics of Interest Lukashenko Arrives in Russia for Talks With Putin The leaders are expected to discuss bilateral cooperation, regional security, and international issues during the diplomatic visit. The Wall Street Journal and Politico, citing their sources, said Ratcliffe also reportedly warned Putin against providing military or economic support to Iran. Around the same time on Wednesday, Trump said that “something may come out of” the visit, adding that his administration was working “very hard to end the war in Ukraine,” despite initially downplaying Ratcliffe’s visit as routine. Russia weighs escalation With peace negotiations reaching a “dead end,” Russia is reportedly considering intensifying ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine. Advertisement Four people close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg on Wednesday that Russia now sees few alternatives to further escalation as it seeks to achieve its military objectives. Tactical nuclear weapons remain as a last resort in the war against Ukraine. “An extreme response is viewed as possible because the only outcome worse than continuing the war for Putin would be losing it,” Bloomberg reported, adding that there is currently no indication that Russia is preparing to use the weapons. Drone incursions raise concerns On Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Chișinău , Moldova for Moldova’s Independence Day celebrations and to meet with Moldovan President Maia Sandu, who said that, prior to the celebrations, five Russian drones had violated the country’s airspace again. Sandu called the incursions “intimidation.” Alongside Sandu, Zelensky is due to hold talks with Romanian President Nicușor Dan as part of a trilateral meeting. On Aug. 17, Sandu said Russia might be deliberately sending drones into Moldova’s airspace, adding that drone trajectories could indicate whether the incursions were accidental or a deliberate test of the region’s response capacity. Advertisement Similar drone incursions have been repeatedly reported over NATO territory, particularly over Romania and Poland in recent weeks, fueling further speculation that Russia may be testing the alliance’s response. At the same time, Russia continues to prepare its youth for a conflict with NATO by 2030. Around 4:30 a.m. on Aug. 16, just a day before Sandu made the remarks, a drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine and flew over the country for 18 minutes before continuing toward Galaţi, Romania. A Spanish F-18 fighter jet on combat patrol shot the drone down. The incident marked the fourth such instance of an intruding drone being shot down over Romania. On July 27, after NATO fighter jets shot down three stray drones over the weekend of July 24-26, Romania ordered a Russian embassy employee to leave the country within five days in what it called a “firm response” to the drones repeatedly breaching its airspace along the Ukrainian border. Russia plans new mobilization On Thursday, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies said Russia is preparing a new mobilization wave that could bring 600,000 additional troops into the war effort in 2026–2027. Mobilization was extended to also include women serving sentences in prisons and penal colonies. According to Axios, Russia’s Foreign Ministry accused the UK and France on Thursday of “playing with fire” by providing Ukraine with technology for long-range strikes, and threatened strikes on British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response. Advertisement According to Bloomberg’s Kremlin-linked sources, Moscow increasingly sees Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO, because alliance members are supplying Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
